overview.title: Chapter 18 summary
overview.chapter: 18 Best practices for the real world
overview.main_topic: Recap of chapter 18: hyperparameter tuning, ensembling, data and model parallelism, mixed precision and lower-precision inference.
overview.central_idea: Getting from a working model to a strong, fast one involves three levers: search and combine better models (tuning, ensembling), use more hardware (data/model parallelism), and use cheaper numbers (mixed precision, float16, int8).
overview.importance: It condenses the chapter's practical advice into a checklist to apply when moving beyond the book's small-scale examples.
learning_objectives: Recall the purpose and main pitfall of automated hyperparameter tuning.
Explain why ensembles of diverse models help.
Distinguish data parallelism from model parallelism and when each is needed.
State what mixed precision and int8 quantization buy you.

summary:
This page is the end-of-chapter summary of chapter 18, "Best practices for the real world." It lists six points:

1. **Hyperparameter tuning** with KerasTuner automates the tedium of finding the best configuration, but beware of **validation-set overfitting**: the more configurations you evaluate against the same validation data, the more the selection itself fits that data (section 18.1.1, p.563).
2. An **ensemble of diverse models** can often significantly improve prediction quality (section 18.1.2, p.570).
3. **Data parallelism** trains one model on multiple devices, each replica processing different batches, as long as the model fits on a single device (section 18.2, p.572).
4. For larger models, **model parallelism** splits the model's variables and computation across devices (p.572 onward).
5. **Mixed precision** speeds up training on GPUs/TPUs, generally at virtually no cost (p.583).
6. **Inference** can be sped up with `float16` precision or even `int8` quantization (pp.582, 585-586).

Read together, the bullets move from improving model *quality* (tuning, ensembling) to improving *speed and scale* (parallelism, lower precision). Note that the summary does not repeat the caveats on float8 (pp.584-585), which the chapter presented as rarely useful outside very large training runs, or the need for loss scaling with float16 mixed precision (p.584).

paragraphs.excerpt: You can use hyperparameter tuning and KerasTuner to automate the tedium
paragraphs.what_it_says: KerasTuner automates searching for the best model configuration, but you must watch out for validation-set overfitting.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Each hyperparameter trial is scored on the validation set; picking the best of many trials leaks information from the validation set into the model choice, so the validation score becomes optimistically biased. A held-out test set evaluated once at the end gives the honest estimate.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Automated search makes it easy to run hundreds of trials, which magnifies this bias.

terminology.meaning: Over-tuning hyperparameters to the validation data, so validation performance overstates real performance.

paragraphs.excerpt: An ensemble of diverse models can often significantly improve the quality
paragraphs.what_it_says: Combining diverse models often improves predictions significantly.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Different models make different errors; averaging their predictions cancels part of those errors. Diversity is the key: ensembling near-identical models adds little.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It is one of the most reliable ways to squeeze out extra accuracy, e.g. in competitions.

terminology.meaning: A set of models whose predictions are combined, e.g. by (weighted) averaging.

paragraphs.excerpt: To further scale your workflows, you can use data parallelism to train
paragraphs.what_it_says: Data parallelism trains a model on multiple devices, provided the model fits on one device.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Each device holds a full replica of the model, processes a different slice of the batch, and the gradients are combined so all replicas stay in sync.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It is the simplest way to cut training time with more GPUs or TPUs, and so to speed up the 'loop of progress' (p.572).

terminology.meaning: Replicating the model across devices and splitting the data between them.

connections: p.572: definition of data vs. model parallelism.

paragraphs.excerpt: For larger models, you can also use model parallelism to split your
paragraphs.what_it_says: When a model is too large for one device, model parallelism splits its variables and computation across devices.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Different devices hold different parts of the weights (e.g. shards of large matrices or different layers) and cooperate on the same batch. Per p.572, it is used to train models that would not otherwise fit, not to speed up ordinary models.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Large modern models, such as the LLMs of chapter 16, cannot be trained without it.

terminology.meaning: Splitting a single model's parameters and computation across multiple devices.

connections: p.572: model parallelism is mainly for models too large for a single device.

paragraphs.excerpt: You can speed up model training on GPUs or TPUs by turning on mixed
paragraphs.what_it_says: Mixed precision speeds up training on GPUs/TPUs at virtually no cost.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Most of the forward pass runs in float16/bfloat16 while weights and updates stay float32; with float16, loss scaling (p.584) keeps small gradients from vanishing.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It is close to a free 2x on supported hardware (p.580).

paragraphs.excerpt: You can also speed up inference by using float16 precision or even
paragraphs.what_it_says: Inference can be accelerated with float16 precision or int8 quantization.
paragraphs.what_it_means: float16 inference is a dtype policy switch (p.582); int8 quantization converts a trained model's weights and matmuls to integers plus scales (`model.quantize("int8")`, p.586).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Faster and cheaper inference matters most in deployment.

terminology.meaning: Running matmuls in 8-bit integers with scale factors.

concepts.name: Hyperparameter tuning
concepts.definition: Automated search over model configurations (layer sizes, learning rates, etc.) scored on validation data.
concepts.intuition: Let a search algorithm try configurations instead of guessing by hand.
concepts.technical: KerasTuner searches a defined space and keeps the best trials by validation metric.
concepts.significance: Saves human effort but risks validation-set overfitting.
concepts.example: Tuning the number of units in a Dense layer.
concepts.misconception: The best validation score from a big search is not an unbiased estimate of test performance.

concepts.name: Model ensembling
concepts.intuition: A committee of experts with different blind spots.
concepts.technical: Typically weighted averaging of predicted probabilities.
concepts.example: Averaging a convnet and a Transformer classifier.
concepts.misconception: More copies of the same model do not make a good ensemble; diversity does.

concepts.name: Data parallelism
concepts.definition: Training replicas of one model on different data batches on multiple devices.
concepts.intuition: Several workers each grade a share of the exams, then compare notes.
concepts.technical: Gradients are aggregated across replicas each step.
concepts.significance: Speeds up training of models that fit on one device.
concepts.example: Training on 8 GPUs with the global batch split into 8 parts.
concepts.misconception: It does not let you train a model bigger than one device's memory.

concepts.name: Model parallelism
concepts.definition: Splitting a model's variables and computation across devices.
concepts.intuition: Several workers each own part of a giant machine.
concepts.technical: Weights are sharded across devices that cooperate on each batch.
concepts.significance: Needed for models too large for one device.
concepts.example: Sharding the kernel of a huge Dense layer across 4 GPUs.
concepts.misconception: It is not mainly a speed-up technique for ordinary models (p.572).

concepts.name: Mixed precision
concepts.technical: compute_dtype float16/bfloat16, variable_dtype float32, loss scaling for float16.
concepts.significance: Speed boost at virtually no cost.
concepts.example: keras mixed-precision policy on a GPU.
concepts.misconception: It does not degrade accuracy meaningfully when done properly.

deeper.title: A decision guide for the chapter's techniques
deeper.body:
- **Model underperforms?** Tune hyperparameters (keep a test set untouched), then ensemble diverse strong models.
- **Training too slow, model fits on one device?** Data parallelism; also turn on mixed precision.
- **Model does not fit on one device?** Model parallelism (often combined with data parallelism).
- **Inference too slow or memory-hungry?** float16/bfloat16 inference; then `int8` quantization for Dense/EinsumDense/Embedding-heavy models.
- **float8?** Only for very large (>5B-parameter) training runs on recent GPUs (p.585).

misconceptions.claim: A higher validation score after a long tuning run guarantees better real-world performance.
misconceptions.correction: The summary warns of validation-set overfitting; confirm on a separate test set.

misconceptions.claim: Data parallelism lets you train models that do not fit on one GPU.
misconceptions.correction: Data parallelism requires the model to fit on a single device; larger models need model parallelism.

misconceptions.claim: Mixed precision is risky and usually hurts accuracy.
misconceptions.correction: The book says you generally get a nice speed boost at virtually no cost.

takeaways: Automate hyperparameter search, but guard against validation-set overfitting.
Diverse ensembles often significantly improve predictions.
Data parallelism for models that fit on one device; model parallelism for those that do not.
Mixed precision gives a training speedup at virtually no cost.
float16 or int8 quantization speeds up inference.

questions.question: When is model parallelism needed rather than data parallelism?
options: When the dataset is very large
When the model is too large to fit on a single device
questions.answer: When the model is too large to fit on a single device
questions.explanation: Data parallelism requires the model to fit on one device; dataset size is handled by data parallelism; CPU and mixed precision are unrelated.

questions.question: What is the risk the summary associates with hyperparameter tuning?
questions.explanation: Repeatedly selecting configurations by their validation score makes the selection fit the validation set.

questions.question: Why does an ensemble need diverse models to help?
questions.answer: Averaging helps only if models make different errors that partially cancel; identical models make the same errors.
questions.explanation: The bullet specifies 'diverse models'; section 18.1.2 explains ensembling.

questions.question: Which two techniques does the summary name for speeding up inference?
questions.explanation: Last bullet. The others are regularization, training-scale, or training-precision techniques.

questions.question: Mixed precision is said to come 'at virtually no cost'. Which chapter mechanisms make that true?
questions.answer: Keeping weights and updates in float32, running numerically unstable ops like softmax in float32, and loss scaling for float16 gradients.

questions.question: For a project of your own, which of the six techniques would you try first, and why?
questions.answer: Open-ended; e.g. mixed precision first because it is nearly free, then tuning.
questions.explanation: Use the decision guide in the deeper section.
